That's true, but that could itself be exacerbated by over-saturation. If Valve's "featured" algorithms need more work, wading through a sea of mediocrity probably makes its job more difficult as well.
It doesn't help that games that area already making enough money are still advertised. Examples include XCOM 2 which was on Steam store's main page for a long time and didn't need any more promotion.
That's a good point. There's a lot of room to better showcase lesser-known but quality games.

One thing I'm sure hasn't helped matters is the fact that virtually every week last year there was a game with Steam trading cards which went on sale for for between $0.09 and $0.19, generally low enough that the money received from selling the trading cards was enough to completely off-set the cost of purchasing the game. Even if the game was complete and utter shit (it usually was), you were essentially out no money out of pocket.

They've since done away with that practice and now during the weekly sales, no game ever drops below $0.49.

Of course Steam probably did away with that practice exactly because there were so many developers abusing it by just publishing paid asset games with little or no functionality. They'd get a percentage of the sales and then a percentage of the card sales too.
